source: 21 CFR Part 211 (with FDA DI Q&A on electronic signatures)
clause: 211.186(a) - Master production and control records: preparation and approval
requirement: To assure batch uniformity, master production and control records for each drug product, including each batch size, are prepared, dated and signed (full signature, handwritten) by one person and independently checked, dated and signed by a second person. MPCR preparation is described in, and follows, a written procedure. Per the FDA DI Q&A, a Part 11-compliant electronic signature satisfies the 'full signature, handwritten' requirement.
system_implications: The MBR authoring workflow requires an Author e-signature ('Prepared'), an independent Checker e-signature ('Checked'; must differ from the author), and QA approval ('Approved', per 211.22(c)/211.100(a)), with an effective date. Versioning and supersession are handled with a redline comparison between versions. Only Effective versions can issue batch records, and in-flight batches stay on their issued version. The MBR is defined per approved batch size. Scaling is allowed only to pre-approved batch sizes, or within an explicitly approved and validated range (see open question), never ad hoc. Changes go through change control with impact assessment.
verification_test: The author tries to sign as checker -> blocked. A Draft MBR cannot issue a batch. A batch size not in the approved list -> issuance blocked. Version history shows who prepared, checked and approved each version and when.

source: 21 CFR Part 211 (with FDA DI Q&A on control of blank forms)
clause: 211.188(a) - BPR: accurate reproduction of the MPCR
requirement: A batch production and control record is prepared for each batch with complete information on its production and control, including an accurate reproduction of the appropriate master production or control record, checked for accuracy, dated and signed. The FDA DI Q&A recommends controlled issuance and reconciliation of blank forms, keeping incomplete or erroneous forms with justification for replacement.
system_implications: A batch record instance is generated only from the Effective MBR version; the MBR version ID and content hash are stored in the instance. An issuance e-signature ('Issued/verified accurate reproduction') is required. Once issued, instruction content is frozen: later MBR changes do not alter it, and any batch-specific change needs a controlled, QA-approved amendment. Batch record instances are uniquely numbered and reconciled (issued vs executed vs voided). Voided or reissued instances are kept with reason and approver, never deleted.
verification_test: Change the MBR after issuance -> the issued instance is unchanged, and the hash still matches the version it was issued from. Issuing from a Draft -> blocked. Voiding an instance keeps it visible with a reason. The issuance reconciliation report has no gaps.

source: FDA Guidance 'Data Integrity and Compliance With Drug CGMP: Questions and Answers' (December 2018)
clause: Q1 definitions: data integrity (ALCOA), metadata, audit trail, static vs dynamic record, backup, computer or related systems
requirement: Data integrity means completeness, consistency and accuracy of data; complete, consistent and accurate data are attributable, legible, contemporaneously recorded, original or a true copy, and accurate (ALCOA). Metadata is the contextual information needed to understand data and must be kept with it. An audit trail is a secure, computer-generated, time-stamped electronic record that allows reconstruction of events relating to the creation, modification or deletion of an electronic record, including record-level and system-level actions. Static records are fixed; dynamic records allow interaction (e.g., reprocessing). A backup is a true copy of the original record kept securely throughout the retention period, including associated metadata, in the original format or a compatible one; this is distinct from temporary disaster-recovery copies.
system_implications: The data model keeps each value with its metadata (units, precision, instrument, specification version, context step, timestamps, user). Dynamic data (trend and historian data, lyophilizer cycles, PAT spectra) is kept in native, reprocessable form with a viewer, not only as images. The backup design follows US-211-68B. The ALCOA attributes map to controls: attributable (unique users, device IDs), legible (rendering, no overwrite), contemporaneous (server timestamps, immediate commit), original (first capture preserved), accurate (validated calculations and interfaces).
verification_test: For sample records, confirm the metadata is complete and the native dynamic data can be re-rendered. Confirm the backup contains metadata and audit trails.

source: FDA DI Q&A (Dec 2018)
clause: Q on validation of CGMP workflows (each workflow is an intended use to be validated)
requirement: FDA expects each CGMP workflow on a computer system (e.g., creation of an electronic MPCR) to be validated for its intended use, citing 211.63, 211.68(b) and 211.110(a). Validating the system or platform alone is not sufficient. (Topic confirmed through secondary summaries of the guidance; the wording is paraphrased from the guidance text.)
system_implications: Validation covers configured workflows, not just the software product: every MBR template or building block, each site-specific configuration, interface and report used for GMP decisions (e.g., review-by-exception rules, release gate criteria, calculations). MBRs themselves need verification (a test or 'dry-run' execution, recipe verification) before they become Effective. This is a validated MBR lifecycle and should be built into the product as an MBR simulation or dry-run mode that produces no GMP records.
verification_test: An MBR cannot become Effective without a linked verification record from dry-run execution. Validation evidence exists for each GMP report and review-by-exception rule.

source: FDA DI Q&A (Dec 2018)
clause: Q on restricting access to CGMP computer systems; system administrator independence
requirement: Access to CGMP computer systems is restricted to authorized personnel. Firms should technically restrict the ability to alter specifications, process parameter data, and manufacturing or testing methods where possible. FDA suggests assigning the system administrator role, including rights to alter files and settings, to personnel independent from those responsible for record content. Where that is not possible, secondary review of settings and content is recommended.
system_implications: Separate administrative (IT/config) roles from GMP data roles, and let no single account hold both at a site by default. Specification limits, process parameters and MBR content can only change through the MBR/master-data change workflow, never through admin tools. Any exception (e.g., a small site where one person must hold both roles) requires documented approval and triggers mandatory secondary review of that person's configuration changes. Privileged activity is logged and reviewed periodically.
verification_test: Try to grant admin and QA/production roles to one account at the same site -> blocked, or requires exception approval. Change a specification limit through the admin console -> impossible. The privileged-activity review report is produced.

source: FDA DI Q&A (Dec 2018)
requirement: FDA is concerned about shared login accounts because they prevent identification of a unique individual, so the system would not conform to parts 211 and 212, and audit trails cannot be relied on to show who entered or changed data when logins are shared.
system_implications: No generic, shared or role accounts for GMP actions, including shop-floor 'line' logins. Fast user switching on shared terminals (badge tap plus PIN/password) makes individual login practical. Machine or service accounts for interfaces are non-interactive, cannot sign, and are attributed to the device or interface. Kiosk-mode terminals still require individual authentication for every GMP entry.
verification_test: Scan the user directory for generic accounts -> none with GMP permissions. A service account attempting a signature -> blocked. On a shared terminal, each entry is attributed to the individual who authenticated.

source: FDA DI Q&A (Dec 2018)
clause: Q on control of blank forms
requirement: Blank forms (including worksheets, laboratory notebooks and MPCRs) should be controlled by the quality unit or another document-control method. For example, numbered sets of blank forms may be issued and reconciled when all issued forms are complete. Incomplete or erroneous forms should be kept as part of the permanent record with written justification for their replacement.
system_implications: The electronic equivalent is controlled issuance of batch record instances, logbooks and ad-hoc forms (e.g., deviation forms, rework sheets). Each instance is uniquely numbered, generated from an approved template version, and reconciled (issued vs completed vs voided). Voided instances stay with a reason and approver. Uncontrolled attachments (uploading unapproved spreadsheets or forms as records) are prohibited; attachments must come from controlled templates or be clearly marked as supporting information.
verification_test: The reconciliation report shows every issued instance accounted for. Voiding requires a reason and QA approval and the voided instance remains retrievable.

source: FDA DI Q&A (Dec 2018)
clause: Q on audit trail review: who and how often
requirement: FDA recommends that audit trails capturing changes to critical data be reviewed with each record and before final approval of the record. Other audit trails (e.g., system-level) are reviewed on a schedule based on system complexity and intended use. Audit trails are part of the associated records, so personnel responsible for record review under CGMP (e.g., 211.22(a), 211.101(c)-(d), 211.103, 211.182, 211.186(a), 211.192, 211.194(a)(8)) should review the audit trails of changes to that data as they review the rest of the record.
system_implications: The MBR designer flags critical data per step (e.g., weights, API lot, IPC results, yields, time/temperature, EM results, label data). The review workbench presents a filtered audit trail of every change to critical data after initial entry (old value, new value, who, when, reason) as a mandatory review section, and QA must acknowledge it before release. Verifiers at step level also see prior changes for the data they verify. A system-level audit trail review (logins, permission changes, configuration changes, failed signatures) runs periodically with a recorded review and outcome. Summary views must not hide individual changes, and full audit trail drill-down is always available.
verification_test: Change a critical value after initial entry -> it appears in the QA release review section and release is blocked until acknowledged. The periodic system audit-trail review record exists with reviewer and findings.

source: FDA DI Q&A (Dec 2018)
clause: Q on when electronic data become a CGMP record (save at time of performance; no temporary memory)
requirement: When generated to satisfy a CGMP requirement, all data become a CGMP record. Data must be documented or saved at the time of performance. Storing data electronically in temporary memory, in a way that allows manipulation, before creating a permanent record is not acceptable; data automatically saved only to temporary memory do not meet CGMP documentation or retention requirements. A LIMS or Electronic Batch Record (EBR) system can be designed to save automatically after each separate entry, similar to indelibly recording each entry contemporaneously on a paper batch record, combined with a procedure requiring entry at the time of performance.
system_implications: Each field entry or observation is committed durably to the server-side record (with audit trail) when the user submits it, not when the page, step or batch is saved. Offline or edge clients (for cleanrooms with poor connectivity) must write to a tamper-evident, append-only local journal with a trusted timestamp and sync to the server without allowing edits in between. Any edit after commit is a change with an audit trail and reason. No 'draft' state for GMP observations that lets values be changed silently before 'submit step'. Data from instruments is captured automatically at generation.
verification_test: Enter a value, then kill the browser or network before completing the step -> the value is persisted and visible with its timestamp. Change it afterwards -> the audit trail shows the original. Offline mode: entries survive device reboot and sync with the original timestamps, and local tampering is detected.

source: FDA DI Q&A (Dec 2018)
clause: Q on electronic copies as accurate reproductions / true copies; static printouts of dynamic records
requirement: Electronic copies can be used as true copies of paper or electronic records if they preserve the content and meaning of the original data, including associated metadata and the static or dynamic nature of the original records. A printout or static record does not preserve the dynamic nature of a dynamic electronic record, so it would fail CGMP requirements as a replacement.
system_implications: Archival and export must preserve dynamic data natively (e.g., historian time-series, lyophilizer cycle data, vision-system images, PAT spectra) together with metadata, not just PDF renderings. Paper-to-electronic scans (for any legacy or hybrid inputs) go through a verified true-copy process (verifier signature attesting completeness and legibility). The originals may only be destroyed if the copy is verified and the SOP allows it.
verification_test: Restore an archived batch and re-render its trend data interactively. A scanned-document workflow requires a true-copy verification signature.

source: FDA DI Q&A (Dec 2018)
clause: Q on electronic signatures in place of handwritten signatures for MPCRs
requirement: Electronic signatures with appropriate controls can be used instead of handwritten signatures or initials in any CGMP-required record. When a regulation such as 211.186(a) specifies 'full signature, handwritten', an electronic signature with appropriate controls that securely link it to the record satisfies the requirement (Part 11).
system_implications: The system may be fully paperless for MPCR preparation, checking and approval, BPR execution and release, provided the Part 11 signature controls (US-11-50, US-11-70, US-11-100, US-11-200, US-11-300) are implemented. Initials fields (e.g., 211.182 'sign or initial') are satisfied by the same e-signature mechanism.
verification_test: MBR approval and batch release are completed end to end with e-signatures, and all signature controls pass their tests.

source: FDA DI Q&A (Dec 2018)
clause: Q on invalidation/exclusion of CGMP data from decision making
requirement: CGMP data may only be excluded from decision making with a valid, documented, scientific justification. All data, including excluded or invalidated data, must be retained and available for QU review; data cannot be deleted or selectively reported.
system_implications: Invalidating an entry or IPC measurement (e.g., a mis-weighed tablet or instrument error) never deletes it. The data point is marked invalid with a mandatory scientific justification, user and timestamp, is visible in the record and the review-by-exception list, and requires QA concurrence where the SOP says so. Statistics show both included and excluded counts. Repeated-measurement ('test into compliance') patterns are flagged, e.g., multiple repeats of an IPC until it passes.
verification_test: Invalidate a value -> it stays visible and marked with the justification, and appears in the QA review list. Three repeats of the same IPC -> an automatic flag.

source: FDA DI Q&A (Dec 2018); FDA Guidance 'Conducting Remote Regulatory Assessments - Questions and Answers' (final, June 2025)
clause: DI Q&A Q on FDA investigator access to electronic records; RRA guidance (FD&C Act 704(a)(4) records requests)
requirement: FDA investigators may review all CGMP records, including electronic records, metadata and audit trails, during inspections. FDA may request records in advance of or instead of inspections (704(a)(4)) and conduct remote regulatory assessments. The final RRA Q&A (June 26, 2025) replaced the January 2024 revised draft. (The investigator-access point is from knowledge of the DI Q&A; the RRA status is confirmed.)
system_implications: Provide a read-only 'inspector view' role (time-limited, audited) with full access to batch records, audit trails and metadata. Provide rapid, complete export packages (US-11-10B) and secure transfer for 704(a)(4) requests. Log what was provided to FDA and when.
verification_test: Create an inspector account -> it can view but not change anything and is auto-disabled at expiry. A records-request package for five batches is generated within the SLA and includes audit trails.

clause: Record integrity architecture: immutability, contemporaneous commit, timestamps, signature binding
requirement: Records must be attributable and contemporaneous, changes must not obscure prior values, audit trails must be computer-generated, time-stamped and retained as long as the record, signatures must be inseparably linked to the records they sign, and backups must be exact and secure from alteration or loss.
system_implications: Engineering judgment derived from the cited rules. Use an event-sourced or append-only versioned record store for GMP data: each entry is an immutable event carrying user, device, UTC server timestamp, site time zone, reason for any change, and a content hash chained to the previous event. The 'current' batch record view is a projection of these events. Signatures reference the hash of the exact record version. A trusted time source (NTP stratum with drift monitoring) must be used, and time-sync failures are alarms. Clock drift on edge devices beyond a threshold blocks data capture. Store UTC and render site-local time with offset (important for multi-site and daylight-saving changes). Database administrators must not be able to alter GMP tables without detection (separation of DBA duties, database activity monitoring, hash verification).
verification_test: Daylight-saving transition test: events around the change keep a correct order and correct displayed local times. Simulated NTP failure raises an alarm and stops capture on edge devices past the drift threshold. DBA-level update is detected by hash verification and database activity monitoring.

meaning: It must be possible to tell who (person) or what (system/instrument) created or changed each piece of data and when; in an eBMR this means authenticated user identity, device ID and timestamp stored with every value and change.
source: EU GMP Chapter 4 draft revision (July 2025), ALCOA++ definitions (definition content confirmed via secondary excerpt). The same term is listed as part of ALCOA in FDA Guidance 'Data Integrity and Compliance With Drug CGMP: Q&A' (Dec 2018) and in the EMA GMP data integrity Q&A (Aug 2016).

meaning: Data must stay readable and understandable for as long as they are kept, and corrections must not hide the original entry; electronically this means human-readable rendering (not only codes) and visible change history.
source: EU GMP Chapter 4 draft revision (July 2025), ALCOA++ definitions (content confirmed via secondary excerpt); also listed in FDA DI Q&A (Dec 2018) ALCOA.

meaning: Data must be recorded when the activity or observation happens, not reconstructed later; an eBMR should time-stamp with a trusted clock at the moment of entry and flag late entries.
source: EU GMP Chapter 4 draft revision (July 2025), ALCOA++ definitions (content confirmed via secondary excerpt); FDA DI Q&A (Dec 2018) uses the wording 'contemporaneously recorded'. Also consistent with current EU GMP Chapter 4 expectation that records are made when each action is taken.

meaning: The first capture of the data (the source record, including its dynamic electronic form and metadata) must be kept, or a verified true/certified copy that preserves full content and meaning; a PDF print of an electronic record is not automatically the original.
source: EU GMP Chapter 4 draft revision (July 2025), ALCOA++ definitions (content confirmed via secondary excerpt); FDA DI Q&A (Dec 2018) phrases it as 'original or a true copy'.

meaning: Data must correctly reflect what actually happened or was measured - free of errors, with edits only through documented, justified and traceable corrections; supported by validated calculations, calibrated instruments and verification of critical manual entries.
source: EU GMP Chapter 4 draft revision (July 2025) ALCOA++ list (exact definition wording not verified in this session); listed as ALCOA in FDA DI Q&A (Dec 2018).

meaning: All data needed to reconstruct the activity must be present - every result including repeats, failures and invalidated values, plus the metadata and audit trail; nothing may be silently omitted or deleted.
source: EU GMP Chapter 4 draft revision (July 2025) ALCOA++ list (definition wording not verified in this session). Also defined in EMA 'Guideline on computerised systems and electronic data in clinical trials' (EMA/INS/GCP/112288/2023) - a GCP document, cited only as supporting EU usage. FDA DI Q&A (Dec 2018) names completeness as part of its data integrity definition.

meaning: Data should be recorded in a uniform, expected way and in logical sequence (e.g., date/time stamps in order, same units and formats), so that contradictions or out-of-sequence entries stand out.
source: EU GMP Chapter 4 draft revision (July 2025) ALCOA++ list (definition wording not verified in this session); supporting EU usage in EMA GCP computerised systems guideline (2023). FDA DI Q&A (Dec 2018) names consistency as part of its data integrity definition.

meaning: Records must be stored on durable, protected media/formats so they survive intact and usable for the whole retention period (backups, archives, format migration without loss).
source: EU GMP Chapter 4 draft revision (July 2025) ALCOA++ list (definition wording not verified in this session); supporting EU usage in EMA GCP computerised systems guideline (2023).

meaning: Data must be retrievable in readable form whenever needed - for review, batch certification, audits and inspections - throughout the retention period.
source: EU GMP Chapter 4 draft revision (July 2025) ALCOA++ list (definition wording not verified in this session); supporting EU usage in EMA GCP computerised systems guideline (2023), which phrases it as available when needed.

meaning: The history of the data - how it was created, changed, moved or where it is stored - must be reconstructable from recorded identifiers and audit trail entries across the whole lifecycle.
source: EU GMP Chapter 4 draft revision (July 2025), which adds Traceable to ALCOA+ to form ALCOA++ (content confirmed via secondary excerpt). Not part of the FDA 2018 ALCOA list.
